opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so when you take a video and break each frame into patches, you end up with a sequence that has two axes of structure: where a patch sits within a frame, and when that frame occurs in time. Spatial attention is the patches within a single frame attending to each other. That's really about understanding the scene at a given moment: what objects are there, how they relate, where the agent is relative to everything else.

Temporal attention is when a patch at a given spatial location attends to the patches at that same location, or nearby, across different time steps. That's where you start capturing dynamics: how things are moving, what changed between frames, and implicitly what action might have caused that change.

The reason you often separate them, rather than letting every patch attend to every other patch across all frames, is partly computational. Full spatiotemporal attention scales quadratically with the number of patches times the number of frames, which blows up very quickly. Factorizing it, doing a spatial attention layer followed by a temporal one, keeps things tractable while still letting information flow across both space and time.

But there's also a modeling argument. Separating them gives the network a useful inductive bias. Spatial layers can focus on the composition of the scene, and temporal layers can focus on change. For a lot of the work we've been interested in, like learning latent actions from video without labels, that temporal piece is really where the signal is, because the action is essentially whatever explains the difference between one frame and the next. So having a dedicated mechanism for reasoning over time ends up being pretty important.

r001.rationale: It says spatial attention lets patches within a single frame attend to one another.

r002.rationale: It says temporal attention lets a patch attend to patches at the same spatial location across different time steps.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way to think about it is that once you've chopped an image up into patches, you really have two different axes along which things can relate to each other. Spatial attention is about the patches within a single frame. You take all the patches from one image, and every patch gets to look at every other patch in that same image, so the model learns things like "this corner of the object relates to that corner" or "the background here is consistent with the background there." It's basically what a standard vision transformer does on a single still image.

Temporal attention is the other axis. If you've got a sequence of frames, like in video or in a trajectory in a game, you take a particular patch position and let it attend to the same position, or really any position, across time. So now the question the model is answering is less "what's around me in this frame" and more "how did this region change from the previous frame to this one, and what does that tell me about what's happening." That's where you capture motion, dynamics, things like an agent moving or an object being pushed.

In practice, the reason you separate them rather than just doing one giant attention over every patch across every frame is mostly computational. If you flatten everything together, attention cost grows quadratically with the number of patches times the number of frames, which gets ugly very fast. By factorizing it, you alternate: do a spatial pass within each frame, then a temporal pass across frames at each location, and stack those blocks. You get most of the benefit of full spatio-temporal attention at a fraction of the cost.

The other thing I'd say is that the two carry different kinds of information, and that matters for what you're trying to learn. For something like learning actions from video without labels, the temporal attention is doing most of the heavy lifting, because the action is fundamentally defined by the change between frames. The spatial attention is giving you a good representation of what's in each frame so that the temporal comparison is meaningful. So I tend to think of spatial as "what is this" and temporal as "what happened," and the architecture is just making that distinction explicit.

r001.rationale: It says spatial attention lets patches attend to other patches within the same image.

r002.rationale: It says temporal attention lets a particular patch position attend across frames, including to the same position over time.

astra-6.text:
Spatial attention is about relationships between locations within an image. If we split an image into patches and treat each patch as a token, attention lets a patch incorporate information from other patches—for example, connecting different parts of the same object. Putting those patches into a sequence doesn’t make that attention temporal; the sequence is just a way to represent the image.

Temporal attention comes in when we have multiple frames, such as in a video. Then we’re relating information across time: how an object moves, or how a scene changes. So the distinction is what the tokens represent and which relationships we’re attending over—positions within a frame versus information across frames. You can separate those two attention operations or attend jointly across space and time.

r001.rationale: It says spatial attention relates image patches to other patches within the image.

r002.rationale: It explains that temporal attention relates information across video frames, but does not specify that it operates at the same patch position across time.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish them by what the model is attending across. With spatial attention, you’re looking at relationships between patches at different locations in an image—how one part of the scene relates to another. Turning those patches into a sequence doesn’t make that sequence temporal; the ordering is just a way to represent the image.

Temporal attention comes in when you have multiple frames and want to relate information across time. So spatial attention helps capture what’s happening within a frame, while temporal attention helps capture how the scene changes from one frame to the next.

r001.rationale: It says spatial attention relates patches at different locations within an image and captures information within a frame.

r002.rationale: It describes temporal attention across multiple frames, but does not specify that it tracks the same patch position over time.
